newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Hanoi sends anti-graft message with trial verdicts.
newsitem.headline: Hanoi sends anti-graft message with trial verdicts.

text.p: Vietnam sentenced four people to death on Friday at the end of a major corruption trial aimed at showcasing Hanoi's determination to stamp out pandemic graft.

Officials and local journalists who attended the trial said Pham Huy Phuoc, former director of Ho Chi Minh City firm Tamexco, was found guilty of corruption and would face a firing squad along with two company executives and a state official.
The remaining 16 defendants received a range of punishments including one life term in jail and two suspended sentences.

Witnesses said Phuoc's girlfriend -- who was sentenced to eight years in jail -- collapsed moments before the final verdicts were read out as police were handcuffing the four condemned men from behind.
Phuoc and the three others remained expressionless as the judgements were delivered.
Friday's verdicts mark the end of Vietnam's biggest corruption trial, but whether the case will now be closed is unclear.
The state prosecution and defence appealed during the eight-day trial for investigators to probe the case further.
Vietnam's state-controlled media, which gave extensive coverage to the case, noted that details revealed in court represented only the tip of an iceberg.
The trial centred around charges that Phuoc and others used their positions in office to siphon off millions of dollars in state funds.
But the political shockwaves go much further.
Tamexco, a Ho Chi Minh City trading firm, was a Communist Party-affiliated company. Several of those implicated have links to some of the most powerful figures in Vietnam.
During their closing arguments, defence lawyers appealed for leniency on grounds that the defendants were victims of a system in which corruption had been allowed to flourish.
"The Tamexco case would never have happened if it had not fallen in an environment where weak state management and irresponsibility reach to the peak," state media quoted one as saying.

Under Vietnamese law, Phuoc and his co-defendants will have 15 days to appeal their sentences. But on the basis of government statements released during the case the chances of a change of heart appear slim.
Friday's Saigon Times Daily quoted a Justice Ministry official as saying tougher measures were being prepared to deal with people involved in economic crime.

The official, Uong Chung Luu, said Vietnam's penal code would be amended to specify stricter sentences for government officials found guilty of corruption, and would outlaw the common practice of civil servants accepting "gifts".
